subject: Creativity
title: Marie Curie: Creativity Against All Odds
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Marie Curie: Creativity Against All Odds.

hook.text: Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. She's still the only person to achieve this.

buildup.text: As a woman in 1890s Paris, she was denied lab space and had to work in a converted shed.

discovery.text: She coined the word 'radioactivity' and discovered two elements — polonium and radium — through years of tedious.

twist.text: The French Academy of Sciences refused her membership because she was a woman — even after two Nobel Prizes.

climax.text: Her notebooks are still radioactive. They must be stored in lead-lined boxes and handled with protective gear.

punchline.text: She changed science so profoundly her notebooks still glow.

quiz.question: Why are Marie Curie's notebooks stored in lead-lined boxes?

details.summary: Marie Curie discovered radioactivity and became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, overcoming extreme poverty, gender discrimination, and eventually radiation poisoning that killed her. Her creative persistence in the face of systemic barriers redefined what was possible for women in science.
details.whyItMatters: Curie represents creative genius achieved despite institutional exclusion. Her story reveals how many potential geniuses history may have lost to discrimination based on gender, race, or social class.
takeaways: Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry
She overcame systematic gender-based exclusion from academic institutions
Her work was done in primitive laboratory conditions with minimal funding

faq.question: What barriers did Curie face?
faq.answer: Women were banned from universities in Poland, forcing her to study secretly. In Paris, she lived in poverty and worked in a converted shed laboratory. The French Academy of Sciences refused to admit her despite two Nobel Prizes. She was nearly denied the first Nobel.

faq.question: How did Curie's creativity change science?
faq.answer: She coined the term radioactivity, discovered two elements, and pioneered techniques for isolating radioactive isotopes. Her work opened entirely new fields of physics, chemistry, and medicine, including the radiation therapy that saves millions of cancer patients today.
